newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO bodes well for finance talks - insurance leader.
newsitem.headline: WTO bodes well for finance talks - insurance leader.

text.p: Success in the next stage of World Trade Organisation (WTO) financial services trade talks could be closer after a successful first ministerial meeting in Singapore, an insurance industry leader said on Friday.
"I think the tone of these meetings bodes pretty well for future talks," Gordon Cloney, president of the U.S.-based International Insurance Council, told Reuters.

Cloney, in Singapore to monitor developments on financial services at the WTO meeting, said he thought responsible negotiating on tough issues had been an important feature of the week-long gathering.

Although no insurance-specific issues were discussed in Singapore, Cloney said he was encouraged by the progress made on the Information Technology Agreement (ITA), which saw countries that had been poles apart at the start of the week come together on an agreed text by the meeting's conclusion on Friday.
Cloney said the way Brazil and India had been brought on board in a number of issues should prove positive when negotiations on financial services resume in 1997.
Both Brazil and India are regarded as having highly influential roles in international negotiations in their regions.

Cloney was also hopeful that the positive momentum of the WTO would be beneficial in the final stages of bilateral insurance talks between the United States and Japan which are due to conclude on Sunday.
"There's some whiskey in the jar now," said Cloney in reference to news this week that Japan was to end its tariff rating system for motor insurance in 1998/99.
Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky left Singapore for Tokyo on Friday to hammer out a deal with Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka.
Tokyo and Washington are at loggerheads over Japan's plans to liberalise its "third sector" for health and niche insurance products ahead of its domestic life and non-life markets.

The third sector, which represents about five percent of the Japanese insurance market, is the only area in which foreign companies have any substantial foothold. Japanese insurers dominate the other 95 percent of the market.
Liberalisation of this sector is seen by international insurers to primarily benefit domestic Japanese insurers.
